title: 《Dune Awakening》创意总监谈借鉴好莱坞、游戏内广告，以及为何风格胜过照片级写实
content:
Dune Awakening's creative director on copying Hollywood, in-game advertising, and why style beats photorealism | GamesIndustry.biz

The fun thing about making a game based on a big movie property is that you get to hobnob with Hollywood royalty. The bad news is that it's through Jira.
Joel Bylos, chief creative officer at Funcom, explains that while making Dune Awakening, the studio had to run various things by Legendary, the company behind the Dune movies. "We submit things to Jira, they approve within a certain amount of time," he explains, namedropping the widely used project-management software that's either an absolute godsend or a relentless destroyer of joy, depending on your personal point of view. "If they don't approve within a certain amount of time, we escalate to them: 'Hey, we need you to approve this'. Usually it's a pretty automated process. It runs pretty solidly."
For Dune Awakening, Funcom has worked with Legendary, which owns the adaptation rights for Dune  |
Image credit:
Funcom
This may all sound disappointingly bland, but that very blandness is the sign of a successful working relationship. Bylos says Funcom has built trust with the film studio, reassuring them that their precious IP was in safe hands. "When you've established that trust, the processes aren't necessarily as important: it's more about just knowing that the other people have the IP's back." Hence the approval process can be reduced to the flick of a Jira ticket, rather than, say, angry phone calls from film executives.
Legendary decides whether to escalate any requests up the chain, such as to author Frank Herbert's estate or to movie director Denis Villeneuve. Bylos says one piece of feedback from Villeneuve was that the game's title "could be a little too close to Star Wars"  – i.e., The Force Awakens – but needless to say, Dune Awakening won through in the end.
All this is a far cry from the lax oversight of licensed games in the last century, when the video game tie-in was often little more than an afterthought. Game and film companies are working more closely together than ever before – and what's really interesting is the idea that game companies could look more like film companies in the future.
The future might see games companies copying Hollywood's production model  |
Image credit:
Funcom
As Code Wizards head Stuart Muckley
outlined to
GamesIndustry.biz
as part of ExDev Week
, the increase in project financing that we're seeing in the games industry (as opposed to firms taking equity stakes in games companies) means that "it's very likely game projects will start to follow a model similar to the movie business, where a legal entity is created for each game." In other words, each game becomes a company.
Bylos can see the sense in it: "You spread the financial risk into a holding company, which is how Hollywood works, right? There's financing per project instead of a company putting everything on the line. So they're like, 'Oh, here's the Dune project, if you want to invest in the Dune project, that's what you do'. But then the investor isn't investing in, say, Funcom necessarily."
It's important to note the above is a hypothetical scenario – for now at least. And Bylos emphasises that there might have to be changes in the games industry if it was to move towards a movie-style model where people are employed on specific games, probably on fixed-term contracts. "I think the Hollywood model works because they have very strong unions," he says. "It's easy for people to be exploited if you don't have strong unions."
Car wash upgrade
Bylos has been with Funcom for a long time: nearly 20 years, in fact. He married a Norwegian and moved to Norway from Australia in the early 2000s. "I found it was quite difficult to get English work – I had to learn Norwegian," he says. "I washed cars at a car rental place for the first three years that I lived there."
"When I was washing cars, I wondered, 'Am I always going to be doing this? Because I have a university degree from Australia'."
Joel Bylos first worked on the game Age of Conan  |
Image credit:
Funcom
His lucky break came in 2007, when he secured a job as a quest designer on Funcom's Age of Conan. He would later become creative director on Conan Exiles, and took on the newly created role of chief creative officer for Funcom in 2019. Right now, his preoccupation is with the launch of PC hit Dune Awakening on consoles, which coincides with a huge update to the multiplayer survival game.
"I think probably the biggest change is the fact that we added a single player mode," he says. In addition, in response to player feedback, Funcom has added various options to adjust the game's difficulty. "It's essentially creative mode from Minecraft," he says. "People want to have the ability to customise their games more and more, I think. It's just becoming kind of standard."
All of this naturally involved a huge amount of work. "Multiplayer balance is completely different to single player balance," Bylos notes. "And then obviously you optimise the hell out of a game for a console. The consoles have different requirements, but there's something nice about having a reliable piece of hardware that doesn't change."
Dune: Awakening - Console and Single-Player Launch Trailer
Watch on YouTube
The console ports also gave Funcom the chance to play around with the haptics and adaptive triggers in the PlayStation DualSense controller. "It's very nice to work with. We have opportunities in Dune that I think fit very well, like the sandworm and the vibrations when you're walking on the sand."
Bylos is hoping that the console launch will bring in a "whole surge" of players, and Funcom has been thinking about how best to keep them playing. "We've been looking at how we push our retention more, things like having more events in the game, keeping people in longer," he says.
